identity.title: Focal deficit screen: facial droop, arm drift, speech (Cincinnati/NIHSS-lite)

technique.how: Rapid structured screen borrowed from the NIHSS: facial symmetry on smile, arm drift over 10 s with eyes closed, speech/language on repeating a sentence and naming, plus a quick check of gaze, visual fields, leg drift, and sensation to each side. Score each item present/absent; any new focal item is positive.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to attend to commands; fingerstick glucose; note baseline deficits and handedness.
technique.contraindications: None; in an obtunded patient substitute observation of spontaneous movement, gaze deviation, and response to pain.

interpretation.positive_finding: One or more new focal items (facial paresis, arm drift, abnormal speech) raises stroke probability roughly five-fold; gaze deviation or hemianopia adds lateralizing value.
interpretation.negative_finding: No focal item present lowers stroke probability (pooled LR about 0.4) but cannot exclude posterior-circulation stroke, small lacunes, or non-convulsive seizure presenting as confusion.
interpretation.pitfalls: Hypoglycemia, Todd paresis after unwitnessed seizure, and hepatic encephalopathy can produce transient focal signs; fluctuating deficits with altered awareness should prompt EEG consideration. In anticoagulated patients any new focal sign mandates urgent imaging for hemorrhage.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: stroke pathway, urgent CT/CTA, reverse anticoagulation if hemorrhage. Negative with persistent AMS or dizziness: pursue metabolic, seizure, and posterior-fossa causes rather than stopping.

estimates.target_condition: Acute stroke, final diagnosis after neuroimaging
estimates.population: Adults with neurologically relevant symptoms evaluated for possible stroke (pooled from studies using modern neuroimaging)
estimates.reference_standard: Final clinical diagnosis after neuroimaging and relevant laboratory tests
estimates.quote: LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1 ... LR of 0 findings = 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25-0.61
estimates.location: Abstract, Results (LR for >=1 of facial paresis, arm drift, abnormal speech vs 0 findings)

estimates.population: Convenience sample of 171 ED and neurology inpatients, 49 with stroke/TIA
estimates.reference_standard: Final diagnosis of stroke or TIA (physician certified in NIH Stroke Scale scored the screen)
estimates.computed_from: LRs computed from abstract sens 0.66 and spec 0.87: LR+ = 0.66/(1-0.87) = 5.08; LR- = (1-0.66)/0.87 = 0.39. Prevalence = 49/171.
estimates.quote: Observation by the physician of an abnormality in any 1 of the 3 stroke scale items had a sensitivity of 66% and specificity of 87%

sources.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.
Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not a rule-out for posterior-circulation stroke in acute vestibular syndrome or for stroke presenting as isolated confusion; a normal screen in those settings needs gait/HINTS or imaging.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: New focal deficit in an anticoagulated patient is intracranial hemorrhage until imaged; activate stroke pathway immediately.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reliability of individual neurological findings ranges slight to almost perfect and improves with standardized scoring (NIHSS); the 3-item CPSS has ICC 0.89-0.92 between prehospital providers and physicians (Kothari 1999).

extraction_notes: This id overlaps substantially with exam_face_arm_speech_cpss; the quantitative base is the same JAMA RCE pooled LR (PMID 15900010) and Kothari 1999 (PMID 10092713). No separate accuracy data exist for an 'NIHSS-lite' bundle with gaze/visual-field items, so the estimates apply to the 3-item core only. LRs for Kothari are computed from abstract sens/spec. Ellipsis in the pooled quote joins two verbatim fragments of one abstract sentence.
